text: The duty of a man is to be useful to his fellow-men; if possible, to be useful to many of them; failing this, to be useful to a few; failing this, to be useful to his neighbours, and, failing them, to himself: for when he helps others, he advances the general interests of mankind.
plain: Be useful to as many people as you can. If you can't reach many, reach a few. Start small and still count.

text: Who dares to tell himself the truth?
plain: Almost nobody. The first lie you hear is your own.

text: Who is there, by however large a troop of caressing courtiers he may be surrounded, who in spite of them is not his own greatest flatterer?
plain: Your own flattery does more damage than anyone else's. You are the biggest yes-man you have.

text: What you desire, to be undisturbed, is a great thing, nay, the greatest thing of all, and one which raises a man almost to the level of a god.
plain: A calm mind is the biggest win there is. Chase it before you chase anything else.

text: We must understand, therefore, that what we suffer from is not the fault of the places but of ourselves: we are weak when there is anything to be endured, and cannot support either labour or pleasure, either one’s own business or any one else’s for long.
plain: Changing scenery won't fix it. The problem travels with you.

text: Neither should you engage in anything from which you are not free to retreat: apply yourself to something which you can finish, or at any rate can hope to finish: you had better not meddle with those operations which grow in importance, while they are being transacted, and which will not stop where you intended them to stop.
plain: Don't start what you can't finish or get out of. Watch for projects that keep growing past the size you planned.

text: We should choose for our friends men who are, as far as possible, free from strong desires: for vices are contagious, and pass from a man to his neighbour, and injure those who touch them.
plain: You pick up the habits of the people around you. Choose friends who aren't run by their appetites.

text: Above all, however, avoid dismal men who grumble at whatever happens, and find something to complain of in everything.
plain: Stay away from chronic complainers. Their mood becomes yours.

text: Are you not ashamed of yourself, you who gaze upon riches with astonished admiration?
plain: Staring at other people's money with wide eyes is beneath you.

text: Look upon the universe: you will see the gods quite bare of property, and possessing nothing though they give everything.
plain: The most powerful things you can picture own nothing. Owning stuff isn't what makes something great.

text: Diogenes, a man of infinite spirit, perceived this, and made it impossible that anything should be taken from him.
plain: Diogenes owned so little that nothing could be taken. You can't be robbed of what you never leaned on.

text: How far happier is he who is indebted to no man for anything except for what he can deprive himself of with the greatest ease!
plain: The freest person owes nothing he can't easily give up.

text: What is the use of possessing numberless books and libraries, whose titles their owner can hardly read through in a lifetime?
plain: A huge pile you never use is just decoration. Own what you actually read.

text: A student is overwhelmed by such a mass, not instructed, and it is much better to devote yourself to a few writers than to skim through many.
plain: Go deep on a few sources instead of skimming a hundred.

text: Let a man, then, obtain as many books as he wants, but none for show.
plain: Buy what you will use. Don't buy to look like you read.

text: Let us then teach ourselves to be able to dine without all Rome to look on, to be the slaves of fewer slaves, to get clothes which fulfil their original purpose, and to live in a smaller house.
plain: Train yourself to live simpler and without an audience. Less stuff, fewer people to answer to.

text: Knowing to what sorrows we were born, there is nothing for which Nature more deserves our thanks than for having invented habit as an alleviation of misfortune, which soon accustoms us to the severest evils.
plain: Habit is a mercy. Hard things get easier because you get used to them.

text: No one could hold out against misfortune if it permanently exercised the same force as at its first onset.
plain: The first hit is always the worst. It never lands that hard again.

text: We are all chained to Fortune: some men’s chain is loose and made of gold, that of others is tight and of meaner metal: but what difference does this make?
plain: Rich or poor, everybody is tied to something. The chain's material matters less than you think.

text: All life is slavery: let each man therefore reconcile himself to his lot, complain of it as little as possible, and lay hold of whatever good lies within his reach.
plain: Everyone is stuck with something. Complain less and grab the good that is in reach.

text: No condition can be so wretched that an impartial mind can find no compensations in it.
plain: There is something to gain even in the worst spot, if you look fairly.

text: Call good sense to your aid against difficulties: it is possible to soften what is harsh, to widen what is too narrow, and to make heavy burdens press less severely upon one who bears them skilfully.
plain: Clear thinking makes a hard load lighter. How you carry it changes how heavy it is.

text: Neither let us envy those who are in high places: the heights which look lofty to us are steep and rugged.
plain: The top looks great from below. It's steep and dangerous up there.

text: Disease, captivity, disaster, conflagration, are none of them unexpected: I always knew with what disorderly company Nature had associated me.
plain: Bad things aren't a shock if you knew the deal when you signed up.

text: How large a part of mankind never think of storms when about to set sail?
plain: Most people head out to sea without once picturing a storm.

text: It is too late to school the mind to endurance of peril after peril has come.
plain: Build toughness before the hit. Once it lands, it's too late to start.

text: Where are the riches after which want, hunger, and beggary do not follow?
plain: Any fortune can be lost. Nothing you own is safe from falling.

text: Know then that every station of life is transitory, and that what has ever happened to anybody may happen to you also.
plain: Whatever happened to anyone can happen to you. Nothing you hold is permanent.

text: Among such continual topsy-turvy changes, unless you expect that whatever can happen will happen to you, you give adversity power against you, a power which can be destroyed by any one who looks at it beforehand.
plain: Look straight at what could go wrong ahead of time and it loses its power over you.

text: They move uselessly and without any plan, just like ants crawling over bushes, which creep up to the top and then down to the bottom again without gaining anything.
plain: Motion isn't progress. You can crawl all day and end up exactly where you started.

text: I will set sail unless anything happens to prevent me, I shall be praetor, if nothing hinders me, my financial operations will succeed, unless anything goes wrong with them.
plain: Plan with a built-in escape clause. Then a setback never blindsides you.

text: Zeno, the chief of our school, when he heard the news of a shipwreck, in which all his property had been lost, remarked, “Fortune bids me follow philosophy in lighter marching order.”
plain: He lost everything and called it traveling lighter. Losing stuff can be a gift.

text: We must take a higher view of all things, and bear with them more easily: it better becomes a man to scoff at life than to lament over it.
plain: Laugh at the mess instead of crying over it. It's easier to carry.

text: So deeply has this evil of being guided by the opinion of others taken root in us, that even grief, the simplest of all emotions, begins to be counterfeited.
plain: We fake even our sadness for the crowd. That's how deep other people's opinion runs.

text: I will never weep for a man who dies cheerfully, nor for one who dies weeping: the former wipes away my tears, the latter by his tears makes himself unworthy that any should be shed for him.
plain: How you face the end decides whether anyone needs to mourn you.

text: Men’s minds ought to have relaxation: they rise up better and more vigorous after rest.
plain: Rest is part of the work. You come back sharper.

text: There is a great difference between slackening your hold of a thing and letting it go.
plain: Easing off for a day is not quitting. Know which one you are doing.

text: “We live a small part only of our lives.”
plain: Most of your days barely count as lived.

text: You cannot find any one who wants to distribute his money; yet among how many people does every one distribute his life?
plain: Nobody hands out cash to strangers, but everyone gives their time away for free.

text: You fear everything, like mortals as you are, and yet you desire everything as if you were immortals.
plain: You're scared like you'll die and greedy like you won't.

text: How late it is to begin life just when we have to be leaving it!
plain: Don't wait until the end to start living.

text: What a foolish forgetfulness of our mortality, to put off wholesome counsels until our fiftieth or sixtieth year, and to choose that our lives shall begin at a point which few of us ever reach.
plain: Putting off the good life until later bets on a date most people never reach.

text: No man knows less about living than a business man: there is nothing about which it is more difficult to gain knowledge.
plain: Being busy doesn't teach you how to live. It may teach you less than anything.

text: You have no grounds, therefore, for supposing that any one has lived long, because he has wrinkles or grey hairs: such a man has not lived long, but has only been long alive.
plain: Old doesn't mean lived. Surviving a long time isn't the same as using it.

text: Balance your account, and run over all the days of your life; you will see that only a very few days, and only those which were useless for any other purpose, have been left to you.
plain: Add up your days. Very few were actually yours.

text: Yet it is easy to arrange the distribution of a quantity, however small, if we know how much there is: what you ought to husband most carefully is that which may run short you know not when.
plain: Guard hardest what can run out without warning. Your time is that.

text: You dispose of that which is in the hand of Fortune, and you let go that which is in your own.
plain: You gamble with what you can't control and drop what you can.

text: Whither are you looking, whither are you stretching forward? everything future is uncertain: live now straightway.
plain: The future isn't guaranteed. Start living today.

text: Our swiftness in making use of our time ought therefore to vie with the swiftness of time itself, and we ought to drink of it as we should of a fast-running torrent which will not be always running.
plain: Move as fast as time does. Drink while the river is running.

text: No one, unless all his acts have been submitted to the infallible censorship of his own conscience, willingly turns his thoughts back upon the past.
plain: People avoid looking back when they don't like what they'd see. Live so you can look.

text: O, how doth excessive prosperity blind our intellects!
plain: Too much success makes you stupid.

text: Since Nature allows us to commune with every age, why do we not abstract ourselves from our own petty fleeting span of time, and give ourselves up with our whole mind to what is vast, what is eternal, what we share with better men than ourselves?
plain: Read the great minds of every age. You can spend time with the best people who ever lived.

text: Those men lead the shortest and unhappiest lives who forget the past, neglect the present, and dread the future: when they reach the end of it the poor wretches learn too late that they were busied all the while that they were doing nothing.
plain: Forget the past, ignore today, fear tomorrow, and you end up busy and empty.

text: Everything for which we are dependent on chance is uncertain: the higher it rises, the more opportunities it has of falling.
plain: The higher you rise on luck, the further there is to fall.

text: We shall never lack causes of anxiety, either pleasurable or painful: our life will be pushed along from one business to another: leisure will always be wished for, and never enjoyed.
plain: There's always one more thing, and rest keeps getting pushed back.

text: When, therefore, you see a man often wear the purple robes of office, and hear his name often repeated in the forum, do not envy him: he gains these things by losing so much of his life.
plain: Don't envy the famous. They paid with their time.

text: Cicero called himself “half a prisoner,” but, by Hercules, the wise man never would have come under so lowly a title: he never would be half a prisoner, but would always enjoy complete and entire liberty, being free, in his own power, and greater than all others: for what can be greater than the man who is greater than Fortune?
plain: A wise person is never even half a prisoner. Staying above Fortune is real greatness.
